Key Message 1...Rain showers, some of the lake-effect variety, end this
early evening and will be followed by fair weather through Wednesday.

NW'erly flow aloft becomes W'erly tonight as a high at the
surface and aloft builds from the central Great Lakes and
vicinity. Primarily fair weather is expected through tonight as
stabilizing subsidence accompanies the ridge. However, the 
passage of shortwave troughs embedded in the NW'erly flow aloft 
and attendant surface trough axes coinciding with weak diurnal 
boundary layer instability will continue to generate scattered 
rain showers across the Eastern Lake Ontario Region and vicinity
through this early evening. In addition, isolated to scattered 
lake-effect rain showers focused generally southeast of Lake 
Ontario, amidst a NW'erly to WNW'erly mean low-level flow of 
sufficiently-cold and moist air over/downwind of the ~23C lake, 
are expected to end by around sunset this evening as lake- 
induced CAPE wanes via a lowering subsidence inversion 
accompanying the ridge. A few lake-effect sprinkles are 
possible generally southeast of Lake Erie through this very 
early evening before ending amidst the waning lake-induced CAPE.
Highs should reach the mid 60's to mid 70's late this afternoon.
The coolest highs are expected in the higher terrain of the 
Western Southern Tier and Eastern Lake Ontario Region. Partial 
clearing and easing surface winds should contribute to lows 
reaching the 50's in most locales around daybreak Wednesday, but
mid to upper 40's are expected in some of the deeper valleys of
the Western Southern Tier and Black River Valley, where cool 
air drainage will complement nocturnal cooling. The efficient 
nocturnal cooling and lingering low-level moisture from recent 
rainfall should result in river and lake valley steam fog, and 
patchy radiation fog, late this evening and especially during 
the predawn hours through shortly after daybreak on Wednesday in
the Western Southern Tier, Finger Lakes, and Eastern Lake 
Ontario Region. On Wednesday, the ridge at the surface and aloft
will begin to exit toward New England and net low-level WAA 
will impact our region along the western flank of the surface 
ridge. The WAA, continued fair weather, and intervals of 
sunshine will allow late afternoon highs to reach the 70's to 
lower 80's.

Key Message 2...Periodic showers and thunderstorms are expected this
Wednesday night through Friday.

During Wednesday night, the aforementioned ridge at the surface
and aloft will continue to exit E'ward and allow a warm front 
to sweep NE'ward through Western and Central NY as a shortwave
trough approaches from the western Great Lakes. The front will
usher-in a warmer and more humid air mass originating over the
Gulf. Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected, especially
after midnight, as weak CAPE, including elevated CAPE, is 
released by the following: moist isentropic ascent along the 
upper-reaches of the front and ahead of the shortwave trough 
axis; low-level convergence/moist ascent along the surface warm 
front. Lows should reach the mid 50's to mid 60's around 
daybreak Thursday as net low-level WAA ahead of and behind the 
warm front and an increase in humidity contribute to a milder 
night.

On Thursday through Friday, multiple shortwave disturbances are
expected to traverse our region generally from west to east. At
the surface, a cold front should sweep E'ward through Western 
and Central NY Thursday evening through Friday morning. Behind 
the front, a surface ridge should build from the Upper Midwest
and vicinity. Late afternoon highs should reach the 70's to
lower 80's on Thursday. Lows should reach the 50's to lower 60's
around daybreak Friday. Highs should reach the 70's late Friday
afternoon as a somewhat cooler air mass overspreads our area
behind the cold front. 

Scattered showers and thunderstorms are expected along and 
ahead of the front as sufficient instability, including elevated
CAPE, is released by the following: moist isentropic ascent 
ahead of shortwave trough axes; low-level convergence/moist 
ascent along surface trough axes accompanying the shortwave 
troughs and the cold front; downshear outflow boundaries 
interacting favorably with low-level vertical wind shear. A few 
severe thunderstorms are possible Thursday afternoon and early 
evening, when moderate deep-layer bulk shear may coincide with 
moderate diurnal destabilization of the warm/moist sector 
boundary layer. The occurrence of severe storms will be 
contingent on multiple factors, including whether enough cloud 
breaks support moderate diurnal destabilization of the boundary 
layer, steeper low-level lapse rates, and greater DCAPE. Behind 
the front, widespread fair weather is expected as stabilizing 
subsidence accompanies the aforementioned surface ridge.
